title: Oxygen concentrator: the oil-free compressor, valves, fans and sensors (only if abandoned)
summary: An oxygen concentrator holds a quiet oil-free compressor, a block of solenoid valves, two cooling fans, flow and pressure sensors and a control board. Allow about 30 minutes. It is also medical equipment that keeps someone alive: strip it only if it is clearly abandoned and nobody needs it. Keep oil and grease off everything on the oxygen side, and discharge the compressor capacitor before you open it.

steps.text: Ask who needs it. A concentrator is a person's oxygen, and a working one is worth more than all its parts. Strip it only if it is clearly abandoned: an empty home, a closed ward or store, with nobody asking for it. If it still runs, take it whole to a clinic, a care home or a household with someone on oxygen. If someone nearby may depend on it, leave it where it is.
steps.warn: Someone with a lung condition can be in trouble within minutes without oxygen. Never take a concentrator from a person who uses it.

steps.text: Unplug it. If it is a portable model, take out its battery first. Wash and dry your hands and put on clean nitrile gloves.

Keep everything on the oxygen side free of oil and grease: the sieve canisters, the small product tank, the tubing, the valve block, the flow meter and the fittings. No oil, WD-40, silicone grease, hand cream or greasy rags, no oily hands or tools, no smoking and no flame, torch or grinder near the machine.
steps.warn: Oxygen-rich air with oil or grease, even a greasy fingerprint, can ignite and burn fiercely. Don't cut, drill or weld the product tank.

steps.text: Stand it on a bench and take the outer case off (screws on the back and under the handle; some are security screws). Photograph the layout. You will see: the compressor (a heavy motor with finned heads on rubber feet), two tall grey or white canisters (the sieve beds), a valve block with coils, a small product tank, filters, fans and the board.

Discharge the compressor capacitor: a small metal or plastic cylinder on or near the compressor. Use the resistor tool from safety_discharge_capacitor, then measure it with the meter before you touch its wires.
steps.warn: A capacitor can hold a charge for days. Don't touch its terminals until it reads near zero.

steps.text: Take the compressor. Photograph and label its wires, unplug them, then lift it off its rubber mounts and pull the hoses off its heads by hand. Cap the ends with clean tape. It weighs a few kilograms and may be warm if it ran recently; wait 30 minutes first. Keep its capacitor with it.
steps.warn: Compressor heads can stay hot for a long time. Let them cool before you handle them.

steps.text: Take the valve block: unplug the coil plugs (12 or 24 V) and unscrew the manifold with its solenoid valves as one piece. Don't take it apart and don't lubricate anything.

Take the cooling fans, the flow and pressure sensors (small modules on tubes with a tiny plug), the control board and the power supply board. Leave the oxygen sensor; it ages out and is of little use.

Leave the sieve canisters and product tank sealed and capped. They hold zeolite pellets and powder, which irritate the lungs and are ruined by damp air once opened. They can go back into another unit, so keep them together with the tubing between them.
Leave used cannulas, masks and tubing: they have been in a person's nose and mouth. Unopened ones are worth keeping. Wash the humidifier bottle with soap and hot water if you want it.

Test the compressor, if you want to know it works. Run it on the bench from a supply it is rated for (see its label; usually 120 or 240 V AC), through a GFCI if you have one, with the wires in insulated connectors and one outlet left open. A good one hums steadily, pushes air from its outlet and doesn't smell burnt or knock. Check the fans from 12-24 V.
steps.warn: Use insulated connections and keep your hands off the wires while it is plugged in. Never run it against a closed outlet.

notes:
## How it works

The compressor pushes air through one of two canisters of zeolite pellets, which hold back the nitrogen. Oxygen-rich gas, about 87-96% pure, passes to a small tank and then to the patient. The valves swap the canisters every few seconds. The compressor is oil-free, so its air is clean.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Oil-free compressor.** A quiet piston or diaphragm compressor, roughly 250-450 W, giving about 1-1.5 bar (15-22 psi) of clean air. Forge or stove air blast, pond or tank aeration, inflating, spray painting, small pneumatic tools that need only low pressure. Never use its air for breathing.
- **Solenoid valves.** 12/24 V valves switching air or water in builds.
- **Fans.** Cooling fans for 12-24 V builds.
- **Flow and pressure sensors.** Small sensors that can be reused with a microcontroller.
- **Boards.** The control board and switch-mode power supply are standard parts.

## Care

- Keep oil, grease and hand cream away from anything you plan to use with oxygen. For air work only, lubrication is not a problem; for oxygen work, assume nothing.
- Don't use salvaged concentrator parts to make oxygen for a patient. Without a purity meter you can't tell if the oxygen is high enough.

## What to leave

- Used cannulas, masks and tubing.
- Sieve canisters and the product tank, unless you are repairing another concentrator.
- The oxygen sensor.
